column4: The section's provision scene begins with Israel delivered from its enemy, then manna and quail sent down; this is the concrete setting for the next ayah's warning about what may descend upon them.
The section's named root غ ض ب and its “upon them” wording meet this scene exactly: after provision, the people are told not to transgress lest غضبي come upon them, and the one it reaches has fallen.
After the fall in 20:81, this ayah turns to God's abundant forgiveness for the one who repents, believes, acts well, then is guided; it supplies the path-finding counterpart to descent into wrath.
In the same calf episode that leads to 20:86, Moses says he hurried to his Lord لِتَرْضَىٰ, “so You may be pleased”; this is a concrete rida counterpart to the later question about divine غضب.
This neighbor to 20:86 names the cause of Moses' angry return: Israel is tested in his absence and the Samaritan leads them astray.

Moses returns to his people غضبان أسفًا, “angry and grieved,” then asks if they wanted wrath from their Lord to descend upon them; the ayah distinguishes Moses' anger from the threatened divine wrath.
After the calf, Moses returns غضبان أسفًا and rebukes his people; this is a second account of the bodily and communal anger scene described in the section.
The calf-worshippers will receive غضب from their Lord and humiliation, while those who repent and believe are then promised forgiveness in 7:153; the ayah stages the section's opposed outcomes.
This ayah joins God's غضب عليه to being farther astray from the middle of the path (أضل عن سواء السبيل), directly linking the section's wrath and lost-way terms.
The ayah asks whether one who follows Allah's رضوان is like one who returns with His سخط; the following and returning actions make the section's approval-versus-wrath relation explicit.
The verse contrasts God's sending فضل upon whom He wills with people returning بغضب على غضب because they reject it; the section's gift and wrath are both something received from above.
The people who were given provisions instead return with humiliation and غضب from God for disbelief and killing prophets; this gives a concrete communal history of favor answered by wrath.
This repeated account says humiliation is imposed wherever the people are found and they return with غضب from God; the verse itself names disbelief and killing prophets as the cause.
This ayah assigns غضب from God and great punishment to those who willingly reopen themselves to disbelief after faith, a concrete opposite to the guided, favored course.
For deliberate murder of a believer, the verse names غضب from Allah, a curse, and lasting punishment; it is another specific case of divine wrath coming upon a person.
The ayah says they followed what أسخط الله and disliked His رضوان; it makes the section's dictionary contrast between wrath and approval an explicit choice of course.
This ayah says God does not approve disbelief for His servants but approves gratitude for them; the difference between rejection and a pleasing response sharpens the section's rida boundary.
This is the command the section quotes: Moses must remind his people of أَيَّامِ اللَّهِ, which the section's dictionary gloss develops as days of punishment for some and pardon or favor for others.
The phrase أَيَّامَ اللَّهِ recurs here with recompense for what people earned; it extends the section's “days of God” from remembered history to a day of accounting.
This neighbor to 4:69 says that obedience would lead to a straight path; it supplies the path immediately before 4:69 names those God has favored.
The section's “those You favored” has an explicit counterpart: Allah favored prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and the righteous, who are described as excellent companions on a shared way.
This ayah names people Allah favored, guided, and chose, then shows them falling in prostration and weeping; favor appears as both a path and a bodily response.
The people of the Garden praise God for guiding them and acknowledge that they could not have found the way without His guidance; this joins the section's hamd, gift, and path.
This ayah speaks of God's completing His favor so that people may be guided, joining the section's root ن ع م to its straight-way frame.
At the end of this long ayah, God says He completed His favor and approved Islam as a way of life; favor and divine رضا meet in one statement.
Here God promises to complete His favor upon the Prophet and guide him to a straight path, directly pairing the section's gift with guidance.
The ayah joins holding fast to God, entering His mercy and favor, and being guided to Him on a straight path; it makes the section's bestowed path concrete.
This divine promise says that whoever follows God's guidance will neither stray nor be wretched; it gives the positive and negative path outcomes behind the section's final categories.
God's guidance is to be followed, with no fear or grief for its followers, while rejection leads to the Fire; this is a direct path boundary rather than a shared word alone.
The ayah explicitly divides people into a guided party and a party that has taken error for guidance, giving a concrete counterpart to the section's path of favor and its lost way.
Neighbor to 20:86: the people explain that they cast ornaments and that the Samaritan cast them too; this gives the concrete action behind the calf episode that occasioned Moses' anger.
This neighbor to 20:86 identifies the calf as a bodily image that lowed and was called their god, the object at the center of the misguidance named in the section.
The next ayah asks whether they did not see that the calf could not answer or harm or benefit them; its helplessness makes the choice of a false guide concrete.
Harun calls the people tested by the calf, names their Lord as the Most Merciful, and tells them to follow him; this is the guidance they refuse in 20:91.
The people say they will remain devoted to the calf until Moses returns, showing the chosen deviation that precedes the angry return in 20:86.
On that Day, some faces are مُسْفِرَةٌ, shining; this is a direct face-state counterpart to the section's favored, softened face.
The same faces laugh and rejoice, adding the visible expression to the section's image of a cool, settled eye.
The other faces have غَبَرَةٌ upon them; the section explicitly links على وجوههم here with its عَلَيْهِمْ wording.
Those faces are covered by قَتَرَةٌ, a darkness that completes the opposite face-state in the preceding ayat.
This day some faces are خَاشِعَةٌ, humbled; the bodily sign corresponds to the low, burdened face in the section.
The opposing faces are نَاعِمَةٌ; this is the same root ن ع م the section names for bestowed favor and softness.
These faces are رَاضِيَةٌ with their striving, linking the blessed appearance to the section's dictionary relation between hamd and approval.
The satisfied faces are placed in a high Garden; this neighbor supplies the setting for the state in 88:8-9.
Their faces show نَضْرَةَ النَّعِيمِ, the radiance of bliss; this directly matches the section's favored face bearing the mark of نعيم.
Some faces on that Day are نَاضِرَةٌ, radiant, a second direct description of the face that bears favor.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord; the neighbor gives their brightness a relation to divine encounter.
The contrasting faces are بَاسِرَةٌ, grim and drawn, the visible opposite of the radiance in 75:22.
These faces expect a calamity to befall them, explaining the grim appearance as a feared outcome.
On the Day some faces whiten and others blacken; the verse makes divergent bodily marks of judgment explicit.
The white-faced people remain in God's mercy; this neighbor names the favorable outcome contrasted with the black faces in 3:106.
Those who do good receive the best and more, and no dust or humiliation covers their faces; favor is visible as an unmarked face.
Those who earn evil have humiliation and faces covered as if with darkness; the verse supplies the opposite of 10:26's clear face.
On the Day, those who lied about God have darkened faces; this is another explicit face-mark of a condemned group.
God saves the God-fearing by their triumph; this neighbor supplies the protected counterpart to the dark-faced group in 39:60.
Moses asks Harun why he did not stop them when he saw them going astray; the wording connects the calf scene directly to the section's ضالّين, those who have lost the way.
Moses asks why Harun did not follow him and whether he disobeyed his command; the exchange continues the conflict between following guidance and remaining with the calf.
Harun says he feared Moses would accuse him of splitting Israel and explains why he waited; the response shows how the episode's communal division shaped his action.
Moses turns from Harun to question the Samaritan, continuing the same calf episode that the section uses to frame anger and misguidance.
The Samaritan gives his account of making the calf; this neighbor supplies the agent's own explanation for the object at issue in 20:86-95.
Moses orders the calf burned and scattered into the sea; this is the episode's concrete destruction of the false object, after his angry return.
Moses ends the exchange by declaring Allah the only God; this closes the calf scene by restoring the true direction against the false one.
After Moses' anger in 7:150, he asks God to forgive him and his brother and admit them into His mercy; the prayer gives the opposite movement to imposed wrath.
Following the calf judgment in 7:152, this ayah promises forgiveness and mercy to those who repent and believe; it names a route back from the condemned state.
Moses' غضب subsides, and he takes up tablets containing guidance and mercy; the ayah separates his human anger from the guidance that follows.
The cloud shade, manna, and quail sent to Israel repeat the provision scene recalled in 20:80-81, placing a gift from above before the warning against transgression.
This neighbor to 2:57 tells the people to enter the town, eat freely, bow at the gate, and ask forgiveness; it joins provision with chosen humility and pardon.
The people change the command in 2:58, and punishment is sent down from the sky; this is the reversal from gift and a route to forgiveness to punishment after transgression.
The Israelites receive shade from clouds, manna, and quail here too; the repeated provision scene helps make the section's warning in 20:81 legible.
This neighbor to 7:160 offers free food and a gate-entry with the plea for pardon, a chosen humility placed beside the later imposed humiliation.
After the people wrong themselves in 7:161, punishment descends from the sky; this repeats the section's pattern of provision followed by wrath after transgression.
This ayah says God does not change a favor bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves; it gives the human choice that can turn a gift into its opposite.
It asks Israel to remember the signs given to them and warns that whoever changes God's favor after receiving it faces severe punishment; the verse directly joins gift and consequence.
The people recognize God's favor and then deny it; this is a specific human response to the bestowed نعمة that the section sets against gratitude and approval.
The verse describes people exchanging God's favor for disbelief and bringing their people to ruin; it gives a concrete reversal from favor to a destructive end.
Every نعمة people have is from God, then adversity touches them and they cry to Him; the verse puts bestowed good and its opposite in one scene.
When favor reaches a person he turns away, and when harm touches him he despairs; this specific bodily response complicates the section's contrast between receiving favor and wrath.
God provides a secure town abundantly, then makes it taste hunger and fear after it denies His favors; this is a communal example of blessing turning to punishment.
The next ayah says a messenger came from among them and they denied him, after which punishment seized them; it names the rejection completing the reversal in 16:112.
After that town's punishment, this neighbor commands people to eat God's lawful provision and be grateful for His favor, returning to the section's positive response.
This ayah describes someone who gives himself seeking Allah's رضا; the active pursuit of approval gives the section's “being pleased” sense a concrete human action.
The verse contrasts a foundation laid on piety and God's رضا with one built over an eroding bank that collapses with its builder into Fire; approval and falling meet in a specific image.
For those who fear God, this ayah promises gardens and purified spouses, then names God's رضا as greater; it joins favor to approval as the section does.
The believers are promised gardens and God's رضا, which the verse calls greater; this gives a concrete positive counterpart to the faces under wrath.
Early believers and those who follow them well are named as a community God is pleased with and who are pleased with Him, with gardens prepared; the path is walked together.
On the Day, truthful people receive gardens and mutual رضا from God; this is a specific day-of-account counterpart to the section's divided faces.
God is pleased with those who pledged allegiance, sends tranquility down into their hearts, and rewards them; their scene makes favor actively bestowed upon a group.
The party whose hearts God writes faith into is supported by Him, admitted to gardens, and mutually pleased with Him; this is another concrete community of the favored.
The God-fearing receive gardens and God's رضا, while God is pleased with them and they with Him; the ayah makes the positive end-state explicit.
This call names a soul راضية, satisfied, and gives the section's رضا a bodily subject at the moment of return.
The soul is told to return to its Lord راضية مرضية, both satisfied and approved; this makes the two-sided approval in the section explicit.
The soul is invited among God's servants, completing the movement from satisfaction to a company on a shared path.
The final command is to enter God's Garden, giving the satisfied soul's destination after the call in 89:27-29.
The account says Hud and the believers were saved by mercy while those who rejected God's signs were cut off; this is a named “day of God” with divergent outcomes.
Salih warns Thamud not to harm God's she-camel or punishment will seize them; the warning begins the Thamud scene named in the section's gloss on أَيَّامِ اللَّهِ.
Thamud hamstring the she-camel and defy Salih's warning, the choice immediately preceding the punishment in 7:78.
The cry seizes Thamud and leaves them fallen in their homes; this is a concrete punishment of the people named in the section's account of God's days.
For Aad, a furious wind is sent over several days so they taste humiliating punishment; this gives a named instance of the punishment-bearing days in the section's yawm gloss.
Thamud are guided but prefer blindness to guidance, then the humiliating punishment seizes them; the verse joins a lost path to a punishment day.
God saves those who believed and feared Him from the punishment in 41:16-17, supplying the contrasting fate within that same historical scene.
The people of Aad deny their messenger and are seized; this starts a second account of the punishment of a people explicitly named in the section's “days of God” gloss.
Aad are struck by a furious wind on a day of continuous misfortune; the day itself becomes the scene of punishment.
The wind tears people away like uprooted palm trunks, making the bodily force of the punishment explicit.
The refrain asks how God's punishment and warning were, closing the Aad scene as a remembered “day of God.”
The account turns to Thamud, who reject the warnings; this begins the second named people in the section's dictionary gloss.
Thamud ask whether they should follow one man from among them, refusing the messenger's guidance before punishment.
They accuse Salih of lying and arrogance; this continues the rejection that ends in their punishment.
God says they will know who the liar and arrogant one is; this is the announced reversal of their claim.
God sends the she-camel as a trial and orders Salih to watch them and be patient; a favor/sign becomes a test.
The people are told that water is apportioned between them and the she-camel, a concrete provision before their transgression.
They call their companion, who takes the she-camel and hamstrings it; this is their chosen act before the punishment.
The cry and punishment follow, directly completing the warning-to-wrath movement.
A single blast leaves them like dry fence remnants; the verse gives the bodily aftermath of the day.
This passage names Thamud and Aad as the peoples who denied the striking event, the two communities cited in the section's gloss on divine days.
Thamud are destroyed by the overpowering blast, one concrete form of the punishment that falls upon a people.
Aad are destroyed by a furious, raging wind; this is the second named community's punishment.
The wind lasts seven nights and eight days, tying the punishment to the section's yawm/day image.
The question asks whether any remnant of the people remains; it closes the scene of a punishment that wholly overtakes them.
The righteous fear a day whose evil is widespread; this supplies the feared setting for the protection and radiance in 76:11.
God protects them from that day's evil and meets them with نَضْرَةً وَسُرُورًا, radiance and joy, a specific positive day-state like the section's luminous faces.
Their patience is answered with Garden and silk, completing the positive outcome that accompanies their radiance in 76:11.
The prayer asks that spouses and descendants be قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ, a cooling or comfort of the eyes, the same dictionary sense the section gives for نعمة العين.
After Mary's childbirth, she is told to eat, drink, and قَرِّي عَيْنًا, “cool your eye”; this gives the section's eye-settling sense a concrete Qur'anic scene.
Pharaoh's wife calls the rescued infant قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ for herself and her husband; this is another concrete use of eye-cooling as joy.
No soul knows what قُرَّةِ أَعْيُنٍ is hidden for the faithful as recompense; the phrase directly echoes the section's cooled-eye branch of نعمة.
After looking, the rejecter عبس وبسر, frowns and scowls; this is the closest Qur'anic facial gesture to the section's dictionary form غضوب, glossed as عبوس.
The God-fearing restrain their rage and pardon people; this reverses the section's dictionary account of anger as boiling blood with a desire for revenge.
Here God punishes the hostile people through the believers, humiliates them, and heals المؤمنين's hearts while removing their غيظ; it joins outward punishment to the inward settling of rage.
When angered, these believers forgive; the ayah uses غضبوا and names a response opposite to the revenge impulse in the section's bodily gloss.
The section's dictionary image links an inner state to an altered eye; here Jacob's eyes whiten from grief, a different emotion but a specific bodily trace of anguish.

Muhammad's companions bow and prostrate, seeking God's bounty and رضا, and the mark of prostration is seen on their faces; this joins the section's favored company, divine approval, and bodily face-sign.
This ayah asks whether the one walking fallen upon his face is better guided than the one walking upright on a straight path; it brings the section's face and path images into one scene.
The condemned are gathered on their faces to Hell and described as farther astray from the way; it directly joins the section's bodily fate to its lost-path category.
The people are called to prostrate on the Day but cannot; the refused chosen lowering of worship meets the imposed outcome described in the section.
Their eyes are humbled and disgrace overwhelms them because they had been called to prostrate while still able; this is a precise reversal of chosen humility and imposed humiliation.

When a man hears news of a daughter, his face turns dark and he suppresses his distress; this gives a concrete facial trace of inner anguish alongside the section's dictionary image of anger showing on the face.
This repeated account again says the face darkens and its owner suppresses anger on hearing news of a daughter, a close parallel to the section's bodily anger image.
This neighbor to the command about أَيَّامِ اللَّهِ recalls God's favor in saving Israel from Pharaoh's people and their torment; it supplies a concrete remembered day of favor.
Moses says gratitude brings increase, while ingratitude meets severe punishment; this links the section's bestowed favor to the choice that can reverse its outcome.
God says He showed the human being the way, then leaves the person grateful or ungrateful; this gives the section's guided path a concrete fork in response to favor.
The Book guides those who seek God's رضا to paths of peace, brings them from darkness into light, and guides them to a straight path; this unites approval and guidance.
God brings believers out of darkness into light, while false patrons lead disbelievers from light into darkness and the Fire; this gives the section's path and two outcomes a concrete reversal.
God names His straight path and commands people to follow it rather than scattered ways that separate them from it; this makes the path boundary explicit.
After a threat, the believers return with نعمة and فضل from God, untouched by harm, and follow His رضا; this gives the section's favored group a specific scene of gift and approval.

The wrongdoers' fire burns their faces when they ask for relief, and the verse calls its drink بئس; this is a bodily punishment and the explicit negative evaluative counterpart to the section's نعم branch.
The Garden's rivers and adornment end with نعم الثواب, a positive evaluative word set against the punishment and بئس in 18:29.
The Garden's people praise God for fulfilling His promise and giving them the land to settle, then call it نعم أجر العاملين; praise, gift, and a good recompense meet here.
The Garden's people say الحمد لله for removing sorrow; the praise follows a bodily settling of grief and God's forgiveness and gratitude.
God sends tranquility down into believers' hearts so their faith increases; this is a specific descent upon the favored group with an inward bodily mark.
The next ayah promises believing men and women Gardens and forgiveness, giving the positive outcome alongside the angry group in 48:6.
God's anger and curse fall on hypocrite men and women and the polytheists, with Hell as their destination; it is a direct group contrast to the believers' outcome in 48:5.
This neighbor to 20:123 names the opposite choice: turning away from remembrance brings a constricted life and gathering blind on the Day, extending the path contrast into bodily consequence.
Whoever is blind in this life is blind in the next and farther astray from the way; it directly joins the section's eye and lost-path details.
The believers who migrated and strove receive good news of mercy, رضا, and Gardens of lasting bliss; the ayah gathers the section's favor and approval terms in one promise.
This neighbor to 9:21 says they remain in those Gardens forever, completing the promised positive outcome.
The contrasting group is promised Fire, God's curse, and lasting punishment; this supplies the condemned side beside the Gardens and رضا in 9:72.
The person gathered blind asks why, though once seeing; this neighbor to 20:124 makes its Day-of-judgment blindness explicit.
God answers that His signs came but were forgotten, so the person is forgotten that Day; this names the choice behind the bodily consequence in 20:125.
The verse says this is how God repays the transgressor who did not believe His signs; it completes the sequence from turning away to punishment.
The same man hides from people and considers whether to keep the child in humiliation or bury her; this neighbor continues the darkened-face reaction in 16:58.
Those who repent, believe, and do good have their evil deeds changed to good, and God is forgiving and merciful; this repeats the section's route from wrongdoing to pardon.
The people of Jonah believe, have the punishment of disgrace removed, and are given enjoyment for a time; this is a concrete community spared after turning to faith.
The verse warns against taking as allies a people on whom God's غضب rests, who have despaired of the Hereafter; it repeats the section's wrath-bearing group.
The Fire scorches the faces of its people and they grimace; this is a direct bodily reversal of the softened and radiant faces in the section.
Those who disbelieve have faces nearly torn by the Fire when they hear the signs; this gives the section's punishment a specific effect upon the face.
The wrongdoer tries to shield his face from the punishment of that Day; this makes the face itself the site of exposure to consequence.
The wrongdoers are brought before the Fire with eyes lowered and humiliation covering them, while believers are in Gardens in the next ayah; it extends the section's visible two-sided judgment.
On that Day faces are humbled before the Living, Self-Subsisting; the ayah gives another explicit bodily state of the judged.
